questions.title: When is prior possession of the same gun treated as intrinsic evidence instead of Rule 404(b) propensity evidence?
questions.question_body: In this felon-in-possession case, two witnesses were allowed to testify that they had seen the defendant with the same sawed-off rifle before the charged night. I thought evidence of prior bad acts or prior gun possession usually raises Rule 404(b) problems. The Eighth Circuit says this was "intrinsic evidence" relevant to proving possession and showing "continuous possession" of the same firearm. What exactly makes evidence intrinsic here, and why doesn't the jury just use it as forbidden propensity evidence?

questions.title: Does the Confrontation Clause issue go away if the out-of-court declarant later testifies at trial?
questions.question_body: Before trial, the defense asked for a limiting instruction so the jury would not treat D.F.'s statements to police as substantive evidence until D.F. herself testified. The government said the officers would only mention the statements to explain their actions and knowledge. The court of appeals then said there was no Confrontation Clause problem because D.F. later testified in person. Is the rule really that a prior out-of-court statement is fine under the Confrontation Clause as long as the declarant appears at trial, even if the jury heard the police version first?

questions.title: Why wasn't testimony about the witness's sister being killed by a gun excluded under Rule 403?
questions.question_body: During cross-examination, D.F. was being questioned about inconsistent statements and said she was not familiar with guns and did not like guns because her sister was killed by one. The defense moved to strike that part, but the district court refused. I would think that kind of testimony could create sympathy for the witness or emotional prejudice against the defendant even though it had nothing to do with this crime. Was the idea that the defense 'opened the door' by asking about her prior inconsistent descriptions of the gun, or is there some other Rule 403 logic here?

questions.title: Why couldn't defense counsel impeach the witness by reading from a police report the witness did not write?
questions.question_body: The defense wanted to cross-examine C.F. using prior statements she allegedly made to a police investigator, but the district court would not let counsel read portions of the police report into the record because the report was not authored by C.F. The Eighth Circuit said extrinsic evidence of a prior inconsistent statement must still be authenticated. I'm confused about what foundation would have been enough here. If the report records what the witness said, why isn't that enough for impeachment?

questions.title: How does harmless-error review work when a defendant claims several evidentiary rulings together made the trial unfair?
questions.question_body: The opinion says that even if an evidentiary ruling were erroneous, the conviction would only be reversed if the jury may have been substantially swayed by the evidence, and it also rejects any cumulative-error theory absent substantial prejudice. How do appellate courts actually apply those standards in practice? If there are multiple small rulings that each seem questionable, when do they add up to reversible error instead of each being dismissed as having only a slight influence on the verdict?

questions.title: How can the § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) enhancement apply based on 'another felony offense' that was never separately charged or proven to the jury?
questions.question_body: At sentencing, the court applied the four-level enhancement for possessing a firearm in connection with another felony offense, even though the defendant was only convicted here of being a felon in possession. The opinion says the enhancement applies whether or not another charge was brought or a conviction obtained, and it relies on PSR facts adopted without objection. What level of proof is needed for this enhancement, and what counts as the 'other felony' in a case like this where the same incident involved alleged domestic assault, kidnapping, and assault on an officer?

questions.title: Why did the district court use the higher offense level from § 2K2.1 instead of the Armed Career Criminal guideline level?
questions.question_body: The jury found the defendant had at least three prior violent felonies, so ACCA applied. But the opinion says the Armed Career Criminal Guideline would have produced a total offense level of 34, while the ordinary firearm guideline plus enhancements produced 35, and the Guidelines require using the greater offense level. I don't understand the interaction between ACCA, § 4B1.4, and the normal gun guideline calculations. Isn't ACCA supposed to control once it applies?

questions.title: Is a claim that the guideline sentence is 'greater than necessary' under § 3553(a) a procedural challenge or a substantive reasonableness argument?
questions.question_body: On appeal, the defendant seemed to argue that applying the four-level enhancement led to a within-guidelines sentence that conflicted with § 3553(a)'s parsimony principle. But the Eighth Circuit treated the issue as: first make sure the Guidelines were correctly calculated, then ask whether the sentence is substantively reasonable. If a defendant says a guideline-driven sentence is too high because it is greater than necessary, is that an argument that the guideline was misapplied, or is it really just a request for a variance and a later substantive reasonableness challenge?
